title: About Time
by: Richard Curtis (writer-director); Domhnall Gleeson, Rachel McAdams, Bill Nighy
summary: A romantic comedy that uses a deliberately simple time-travel rule to turn, halfway through, into a family drama about a dying father and the value of living an ordinary day.

title: Amour
by: Michael Haneke (writer-director); Darius Khondji (cinematography); Jean-Louis Trintignant, Emmanuelle Riva, Isabelle Huppert
summary: A chamber film that shows its ending first, so that every quiet domestic scene in one Paris apartment becomes dread, and lets long takes, offscreen sound and the absence of any score carry a love story through illness to death.

title: Autumn Sonata
by: Ingmar Bergman (writer-director); Sven Nykvist (cinematography); Ingrid Bergman, Liv Ullmann, Lena Nyman
summary: A chamber film in which one Chopin prelude, played first by a daughter and then by her famous mother, holds a whole relationship, and a single night of talk becomes the climax.

title: Boyhood
by: Richard Linklater (writer-director); Ellar Coltrane, Patricia Arquette, Ethan Hawke, Lorelei Linklater
summary: Shot over twelve years with the same cast, it shows a coming-of-age story built from ellipses and near-misses instead of plot turns, with the actors' real ageing doing the work of a timeline.

title: Feel Good
by: Mae Martin and Joe Hampson (creators, writers); Mae Martin, Charlotte Ritchie, Lisa Kudrow, Sophie Thompson, Phil Burgers
summary: A semi-autobiographical romcom in which love is the new addiction, a stand-up stage is where pain becomes material, and the real wound is withheld until the second and final series.

title: Fleabag
by: Phoebe Waller-Bridge (writer, star); Harry Bradbeer (director); Sian Clifford, Olivia Colman, Andrew Scott, Bill Paterson
summary: A comedy that turns its heroine's asides to camera into both her armour and, in a six-episode romance with a priest, the thing she has to give up.

title: Force Majeure
by: Ruben Östlund (writer-director); Fredrik Wenzel (cinematography); Johannes Kuhnke, Lisa Loven Kongsli, Kristofer Hivju, Fanni Metelius
summary: A marriage comedy built on a three-second inciting incident, in which a father's flight from an avalanche becomes an argument nobody can settle, played out in long, static, excruciating takes.

title: I May Destroy You
by: Michaela Coel (creator, writer, star, co-director); Sam Miller (co-director); Weruche Opia, Paapa Essiedu
summary: A drama built around a rape its heroine can't remember, which tells one night across twelve episodes, widens it into a study of consent, and ends with several endings instead of one.

title: La Haine
by: Mathieu Kassovitz (writer-director); Pierre Aïm (cinematography); Vincent Cassel, Hubert Koundé, Saïd Taghmaoui
summary: A day-long countdown with on-screen clock times, framed by a parable told at the start and the end, that shows how a gun planted early, three foils and a ticking clock can make idle hours feel like a fall.

title: La La Land
by: Damien Chazelle (writer-director); Justin Hurwitz (music); Benj Pasek and Justin Paul (lyrics); Linus Sandgren (cinematography); Tom Cross (editing); Emma Stone, Ryan Gosling, John Legend
summary: A musical that uses the seasons as chapters, gives each lover an "I want" song, and ends with a montage of the life they didn't live, making dream and love the two sides of one trade-off.

title: La Notte
by: Michelangelo Antonioni (director); Gianni Di Venanzo (cinematography); Giorgio Gaslini (music); Marcello Mastroianni, Jeanne Moreau, Monica Vitti
summary: A day and a night in a dying marriage, told almost entirely through images: figures dwarfed by Milan's new architecture, faces behind glass, a long silent walk, and a dawn ending that withholds the climax.

title: The Lord of the Rings
by: Peter Jackson (director); screenplays by Fran Walsh, Philippa Boyens and Peter Jackson (with Stephen Sinclair on The Two Towers), from J. R. R. Tolkien; music by Howard Shore
summary: A nine-hour quest that braids three strands toward one fixed destination, restructures its source with care, lets leitmotifs carry memory, and ends with a hero who cannot go home.

title: Nights of Cabiria
by: Federico Fellini (director, co-writer with Ennio Flaiano and Tullio Pinelli; dialogue help from Pier Paolo Pasolini); Nino Rota (music); Giulietta Masina
summary: An episodic film held together by one indomitable face, whose opening betrayal predicts its ending, and whose last shot, a look straight into the lens, turns survival into a question for the audience.

title: Prometheus
by: Ridley Scott (director); screenplay by Jon Spaihts and Damon Lindelof; Michael Fassbender, Noomi Rapace, Charlize Theron
summary: An honest double lesson: superb design, a model character introduction in David and a set piece built on a want under pressure, undermined by decisions that come from the plot rather than the characters.

title: Rosemary's Baby
by: Roman Polanski (writer-director, from Ira Levin's 1967 novel); William Castle (producer); William Fraker (cinematography); Krzysztof Komeda (music); Mia Farrow, John Cassavetes, Ruth Gordon, Sidney Blackmer
summary: A horror film built almost entirely on restricted point of view and domestic dread, which keeps every clue ambiguous until an ending that turns the genre's confrontation into acceptance.

title: Sorry, Baby
by: Eva Victor (writer-director-star); Naomi Ackie, Lucas Hedges, John Carroll Lynch
summary: A comedy-drama about the years after a sexual assault that never shows the assault, tells its story in out-of-order 'The Year with…' chapters, and lets jokes and small kindnesses carry the pain.

title: Spirited Away
by: Hayao Miyazaki (writer-director), Studio Ghibli; music by Joe Hisaishi
summary: A coming-of-age fantasy whose heroine grows through work and kindness rather than combat, set in a bathhouse whose rules are the plot, with Miyazaki's deliberate pauses (ma) doing as much as the action.

title: Succession
by: Jesse Armstrong (creator, showrunner); Mark Mylod (director of key episodes); Brian Cox, Jeremy Strong, Kieran Culkin, Sarah Snook, Matthew Macfadyen
summary: An ensemble tragedy told as comedy, worth studying for a status game that escalates into humiliation and a patriarch's death heard only down a phone line, shot in one long take.

title: Taste of Cherry
by: Abbas Kiarostami (writer-director); Homayoun Ershadi, Abdolrahman Bagheri
summary: A road film reduced to a car, three passengers and one request, which withholds its hero's reasons and its own ending, then breaks the frame with video of the crew.

title: The Sopranos
by: David Chase (creator); James Gandolfini, Edie Falco, Lorraine Bracco; HBO, 1999–2007
summary: A gangster story turned inside out by a therapy frame, which keeps us aligned with a murderer for six seasons, tests that allegiance from the fifth episode on, and ends by refusing to tell us how it ends.

title: The Square
by: Ruben Östlund (writer-director); Claes Bang, Elisabeth Moss, Dominic West, Terry Notary
summary: An episodic satire whose A and B stories rhyme around one question (what we owe strangers), climaxing in a gala-dinner performance where a room of bystanders fails to move.

title: Tony
by: Matt Johnson (director, co-writer); Dominic Sessa, Antonio Banderas, Leo Woodall, Emilia Jones; A24
summary: A biopic that refuses to be one: it shrinks Anthony Bourdain's life to a single invented-and-compressed summer in a Provincetown kitchen, turning a famous man into a coming-of-age story and raising sharp questions about how far a true story may bend.

title: Uptown Girls
by: Boaz Yakin (director); Brittany Murphy, Dakota Fanning, Heather Locklear
summary: A critically panned but much-loved odd-couple film in which a childlike heiress and an adult-like eight-year-old swap what each lacks, built on Snyder's Buddy Love and a teacup ride that pays off a plant.

title: The Virgin Suicides
by: Sofia Coppola (writer-director, from Jeffrey Eugenides's 1993 novel); Ed Lachman (cinematography); Air (score); Kirsten Dunst, James Woods, Kathleen Turner, Josh Hartnett; Giovanni Ribisi (narrator)
summary: A film narrated by a collective "we" that tells its outcome in the first minutes, turning suspense into elegy and showing how memory makes a myth of people it never understood.

title: Whiplash
by: Damien Chazelle (writer-director); Tom Cross (editing); Sharone Meir (cinematography); Justin Hurwitz (music); Miles Teller, J. K. Simmons, Paul Reiser, Melissa Benoist
summary: A two-hander that escalates like a fight, cut to the rhythm of its music, whose triumphant final performance leaves audiences arguing over whether it endorses the abuse that produced it.

title: World War Z
by: Marc Forster (director); screenplay by Matthew Michael Carnahan, Drew Goddard and Damon Lindelof, from the novel by Max Brooks; Brad Pitt, Mireille Enos
summary: A zombie epic rebuilt as a globe-trotting investigation, whose scrapped battle finale was replaced by a near-silent climax in a lab corridor: a lesson in sequences, scale versus intimacy, and adapting an oral history into a single hero's quest.

title: The Worst Person in the World
by: Joachim Trier (director; co-writer with Eskil Vogt); Renate Reinsve, Anders Danielsen Lie, Herbert Nordrum
summary: A coming-of-age film told in a prologue, twelve titled chapters and an epilogue, whose wry narrator, elastic sense of time and a city frozen mid-stride show how the telling can carry a heroine who won't choose.

title: Yi Yi
by: Edward Yang (writer-director); Wu Nien-jen, Elaine Jin, Kelly Lee, Jonathan Chang
summary: A three-hour family ensemble framed by a wedding and a funeral, where cross-cut first loves and a boy photographing the backs of people's heads show how much a story can hold without a single protagonist.
